about: A test of the flight look on one page of the Wang Bi lesson, before changing the lesson. The user, 2026-09-27, on what they liked in Alien's screens: 'There was sound effects, there was vector graphics, there was movement and panning and zoom. It was transporting you into a specific view of the world, which is in the infographic.' See docs/research/2026-09-27-nostromo-screens.md. The view approaches 22 while its lines plot (a relay click each), goes down to L5 as the answer types (a printer's chatter), then circles the upper trigram; a hum under the music; the screen pushed in on slowly, with a light bloom. Round 2, the user: 'boost the sound and take out the music and see what it's like.' Round 3, the user on the 12 s hold: 'there is some dead space or sound at the end ... should we just cut to the six lines ... scene?' Hold 5 s, then the end card. Round 4: the bow and blur smeared the scan lines and pixel font (the user: 'It's not pixelated. I can't see the scan lines'); now bloom only, and not on the end card. Round 6, the user: 'no sound at all is a bit lacking ... in the Nostromo, we had some background buzz.' The 50-150 Hz hum was lost on a phone; a mid-range bed replaces it (air, buzz, chirps). This is the version without music; wangbi-flight-test-music has the music at a third, up at the edges. Round 7, the user on the chirps: 'Those chirps are very annoying.' Measured against YouTube references (docs/research/2026-09-27-sound-measures.md), the bed is rebuilt after the Nostromo's landing on LV-426, the user's pick: engine rumble swelling every 6 s, its 250 Hz-1 kHz body turned up for phones, a quiet 440 Hz whine, no chirps; and a beacon, one beep at about 1.2 kHz on a steady 1.65 s pulse, rising slowly, no louder than the bed.
